Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "P=1.6", Sentence = "As a further sensitivity test we confirmed that mKFG int retained positive incremental discrimination over the eGFRcr, age and sex baseline within strata of age, sex, diabetes status and baseline kidney function, with its prognostic effect strongest where creatinine-based eGFR is least informative (HR 0.59 per SD for eGFR ≥60 versus 0.82 for eGFR <60; mKFG int × eGFR interaction P=1.6×10⁻⁵; Suppl.Table.6)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Kidney disease is a rapidly growing global health concern, tightly linked to cardiovascular and metabolic disease within the recently defined cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome.

Routine clinical assessment of kidney function primarily relies on creatinine-based estimated glomerular filtration rates (eGFRcr) which can be affected by non-renal factors and declines only after substantial kidney damage.
Using data from the MetaCardis study (N=1,723), we derived metabolomic kidney function gaps (mKFGs)-the difference between metabolome-predicted eGFRcr and measured eGFRcr.

A physiologyguided feature-selection strategy -anchored on three cardiometabolic markers (haemoglobin, albumin and the Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte Ratio) that associate with mKFGs but not with eGFRcr -yielded compact sex-stratified metabolite panels (40-98 out of 1,514 metabolites) that tracked cardiovascularkidney-metabolic risk.
Machine-Learning models revealed distinct metabolic signatures, including biomarkers of meat consumption and androgens, highlighting potential sex-specific pathways linked to CKM health.

External validation in the general-population Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (N=9,958) and German Chronic Kidney Disease Study (N=5,113) cohorts revealed that mKFGs added incremental predictive value for future CKM events and all-cause mortality beyond eGFRcr and established risk equations.
Our findings open new avenues for personalised risk stratification for CKM disease progression and targeted interventions based on metabolically defined kidney health.

text.text: We also uncover sex-specific metabolome signatures predictive of kidney function, offering insights into purported mechanistic differences in CKM physiology between sexes.

To expedite translation, we use a physiology-guided feature selection strategy to devise generalisable and sex-specific metabolomic panels (40-98 serum metabolites) that outperform models using all available metabolites.

Our work suggests application of ML algorithms and serum metabolites for monitoring risk of future cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic events and informs mechanistic and clinical studies to uncover the role of metabolic perturbations in CKM health.

We determined that, in addition to a cohort representative of the general population, mKFGs could detect future CKM outcomes in a mild-to-moderately severe CKD population with intersected metabolite panels consistently outperforming mKFGs from all metabolites and significantly improving performance of models containing eGFRcr, uACR or established scores of CKM risk in both sexes.

By harnessing the ability of ML algorithms to detect patterns in high dimensional data, we derived personalised metabolomic kidney function gaps (mKFGs) from ML-based eGFR predictions using circulating metabolites as input. mKFGs reliably distinguished baseline kidney and associated cardiometabolic health status and predicted future CKM disease trajectories across three independent cohorts of varying study designs and kidney disease burden totaling 16,794 participants.

These cohorts were chosen to span the cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic disease spectrum, from a general population without overt CKD (CLSA) to an established CKD population at high cardiovascular risk (GCKD), allowing us to test whether a single baseline score predicts future CKM events across this range.

Using a physiology-guided feature selection strategy, we optimised serum metabolite panels for men, women and all participants and captured CKM health status and risk more effectively than using all metabolites, creatinine-based eGFR and established risk scores only.

Despite extensive adjustment for multiple kidney health-related covariates (age, sex, eGFR, uACR), clinical risk scores (FRS, KFRE) and use of more precise method to estimate GFR (eGFR cys ), models including mKFGs improved classification of individuals across CKM trajectories.
Anchoring our metabolomic prediction on eGFRcr leverages an already CKM-relevant starting point rather than refining pure glomerular filtration.
The physiology-guided optimisation toward haemoglobin, albumin and NLR -CKM-axis variables uncorrelated with eGFRcr in MetaCardis -extends this CKM-sensitivity beyond what eGFRcr alone captures.

These findings imply that mKFGs are not merely refined estimates of GFR -that is, a risk-enriched metabolomic deviation from creatinine-based kidney filtration -but rather represent, by integrating metabolic signals, a multifaceted score of kidney and associated cardiometabolic health independently of existing markers.

Specifically, mKFG int inclusion, improved patient discrimination (from 0.012 (stroke) to 0.032 (all-cause mortality)) and reclassification (up to 38.5% for all-cause mortality) for cardiovascular outcomes comparable to those previously reported with proteome-based models 69, 70 underscoring the interplay between kidney and cardiovascular health.

text.text: Despite omics-based risk scores often improving patient classification, their adoption in clinical practice is often hindered by their complexity and costs.

The optimised metabolomic panels we derived, by reducing the metabolomic space required to monitor CKM health by up to 40-fold combined with improvements in automated sample preparation and metabolite annotation could pave the way to overcome some of these limitations.

A comparable path, from broad discovery to a compact clinically deployed test, has recently been realised in liver disease, where a serum panel of 12 lipids combined with routine clinical measures can prioritise patients at risk of steatohepatitis 74, 75 .
text.formatted: A comparable path, from broad discovery to a compact clinically deployed test, has recently been realised in liver disease, where a serum panel of 12 lipids combined with routine clinical measures can prioritise patients at risk of steatohepatitis <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">74,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">75</ref> .

text.text: Similarly, our work could serve as a paradigm for further development of selective metabolome-informed scores for clinical assessment of CKM health allowing for personalised risk stratification and early intervention.

Early detection of individuals at higher CKM risk is particularly important, since new-generation anti-diabetic drugs (Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor analogs and Sodium-glucose Transport Protein 2 inhibitors) which have documented renoprotective properties [76] [77] [78] may help preserve kidney function if initiated early.

text.text: Our findings could facilitate early detection of individuals at high risk of AKI, the most prevalent renal exacerbation event in patients with CKD, commonly leading to severe complications with high mortality 79 , allowing for targeted clinical vigilance and medication management.

text.text: Our study has some limitations.

Our cohorts predominantly consisted of white participants albeit from varying geographical and environmental backgrounds (Europe and North America), questioning the generalisability of our findings across other ancestries.

Additionally, we primarily relied on linear modelling to derive kidney function gaps and whilst a non-linear ML method in our training cohort did not confer appreciable benefits, non-linear ML could potentially further improve our approach particularly as computational power increases in the future.
Untargeted metabolomics typically provide relative metabolite quantifications rather than absolute concentrations, preventing us from establishing universal reference concentrations.
Devising targeted quantitative assays for our optimised metabolite panels, along with prospective validation, is an essential next step towards clinical application.

Importantly, the relationships we report between mKFGs and cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic health are observational associations and do not, in themselves, establish causal or physiological mechanisms.
The biological interpretations we offer for individual metabolites and pathways are therefore hypothesisgenerating and warrant dedicated experimental validation.

The lack of serial metabolomic measurements in our cohorts precluded direct assessment of whether mKFGs change over time in response to disease progression, lifestyle modification, or therapeutic intervention; this remains to be evaluated in cohorts or trials with serial metabolomic profiling.

Additionally, urine metabolome data were not available across all three cohorts, so we could not test whether urinary metabolomics might 477 outperform or complement the serum metabolome as a readout of CKM health.
This remains a 478 promising avenue for future work.

Finally, like other omics-derived scores, our current panels rely on 479 high-throughput metabolomics platforms that are not yet widely accessible and currently limit 480 deployment in low-resource settings.
Further reduction to compact, targeted assays, along with 481 validation in ancestrally diverse cohorts will be needed to broaden accessibility.

To conclude, we demonstrate that leveraging ML with circulating metabolite profiles can refine 483 estimates of CKM health and improve risk prediction of future CKM diseases beyond widely adopted 484 clinical markers.

Our work sets the stage for developing noninvasive tests to monitor CKM disease risk 485 and informs future mechanistic and clinical studies aiming to preserve kidney function in both the 486 general and the CKD population.

text.text: Overt CKD was an exclusion criterion in MetaCardis and we therefore postulated that training eGFR-predicting models in MetaCardis would capture kidney functional heterogeneity in the presence of common co-morbidities and would better generalise in independent cohorts.
We employed bootstrap aggregation for model training and nested fivefold crossvalidation to optimise the L1 regularization parameter, λ.
Initially, we split our MetaCardis cohort into 5 equal parts with 4/5 as the training set and 1/5 as the test (left-out) set and mean-centred and varianceadjusted (z-scored) the input variables.

We next used fivefold cross-validation in the training set (80% of participants) to determine the optimal regularization parameter lambda (from 200 values ranging from 10 -2 to 10 1 ) for predicting eGFR.
We used the optimal λ to train a Lasso regression model in the training set and predicted eGFR in the left-out group (20% of the cohort).

This process was repeated for each of the other four equal parts of the cohort, resulting in a predicted eGFR value for each participant which was then used to calculate the coefficient of determination using the rsq function from yardstick (v0.0.7) and an averaged β-coefficient from five models in each training split for each input variable.
To account for cohort heterogeneity the process was repeated 100 times and the mean predicted eGFR and βcoefficients from all ensemble models were used in all subsequent analyses.
In separate analyses, to exclude chance-biased predictions, eGFR was randomly permuted in the left-out group and predicted with metabolomics as input in all three studied cohorts, as indicated.

For metabolomics, which was the data modality best explaining eGFRcr variance, we also trained models in MetaCardis with 1,276 metabolites common between MetaCardis and CLSA; and with 1,152 metabolites common between MetaCardis, CLSA and GCKD, to predict z-scored eGFR (to account for different eGFR distributions between cohorts).
We then used these models to predict eGFR in CLSA (N = 9,958) or GCKD (N=5,113) participants with available baseline metabolomics, as applicable.

Metabolite intensities were z-scored within each cohort separately prior to modelling; the MetaCardis-trained models were applied to identically z-scored CLSA and GCKD data, without further cross-platform rescaling and without information leakage between cohorts.

To assess the robustness and reproducibility of the top metabolite selections, the eGFRcr-prediction Lasso ensemble (100 iterations, nested 5-fold cross-validation) was retrained de novo in CLSA on the 1,276 metabolites common to MetaCardis and CLSA, and per-metabolite selection frequencies were compared between the two cohort-specific ensembles.

To uncover sex-specific metabolite panels relevant to kidney health we also performed model training as above exclusively in men or women participating in MetaCardis participants and predicted z-scored eGFR in males or females in CLSA or GCKD.

To calculate personalized metabolomic kidney function gaps (mKFGs) for each participant of the three studies, conventional creatinine-based eGFRcr was subtracted from eGFR predictions of models trained in MetaCardis on serum metabolomics, as applicable.

This is conceptually similar to proteomic ageing gaps 11 and multi-omic BMI signatures 18, 19 , defined as the numerical difference between a clinical reference variable and an omics-derived prediction of that variable.

To discover metabolites strengthening associations with cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic phenotypes we adapted the permutation feature importance (PFI) method 99 , as further refined by Oh and colleagues for health-relevant outcomes 11 .

text.text: We did not seek to identify metabolites that after permutation decrease the accuracy of predicted eGFRcr but instead focused on permuted metabolites that modify association between kidney gaps (predicted minus eGFRcr) with biochemical variables indicative of CKM health.

In the absence of a universally accepted score of kidney health and biochemical metrics of kidney function (uACR, urea, urate, cystatin C, calcium phosphate) in our non-CKD cohorts (MetaCardis and CLSA), we optimised our models in MetaCardis with serum haemoglobin, serum albumin or the Neutrophil-to-Lymphocyte ratio as the target variables.
These variables were selected in a data-driven way due to their association with mKFGall but not eGFRcr (Fig. 2E).

text.text: We reasoned that optimising our models towards these variables could integrate and reflect interlinked multi-organ information relevant to CKM health independently to that already contained in eGFRcr.

A metabolite that after its permutation in the test set, kidney gaps using the resulting eGFR prediction after correcting for age, sex, creatinine-based eGFR and centre of recruitment, exhibited diminished Spearman ρ with the target variable than gaps without permutation, was deemed relevant in capturing associations between gaps and target variable.

The feature importance (FI) score for each metabolite was calculated as the % difference between partial Spearman ρ between the target variable and the kidney gaps with or without permutation and was used to rank metabolites.

In GCKD, study entry was defined as the time origin and the time scale was time since study entry; follow-up was restricted to the first 8.5 years after baseline.

Participants who did not experience the event of interest were censored at the earliest of: date last known alive, date of death from causes unrelated to the event of interest, or 8.5 years after baseline.

To test whether mKFGint reflects more than improved filtration estimation, we derived a metabolomebased GFR estimate (eGFR_metF) in CLSA using the creatinine-and demographics-free metabolite equation of Coresh et al. (2019)  66 : eGFR_metF = exp(3.04584 -0.450817•ln[N-acetylthreonine] -0.214876•ln[pseudouridine] -0.253004•ln[myo-inositol] + 0.2265693•ln[tryptophan]), applied to the batch-normalised relative metabolite abundances.

(A) Analysis strategy.
(1) The MetaCardis discovery cohort (n = 1,723) spans the cardiometabolic spectrum from healthy individuals to obesity/metabolic syndrome, type 2 diabetes and ischaemic heart disease.
(2) Of ten data modalities compared, the serum metabolome (1,514 metabolites) was the best single predictor of creatinine-based eGFR (eGFRcr).
(3) A nested 5-fold cross-validation (80% train / 20% test, 100 bootstrap iterations) was used to predict eGFRcr via Lasso, giving an averaged predicted eGFRcr per participant.

(4) The metabolomic kidney function gap is defined as mKFG = predicted minus calculated eGFRcr, residualised on baseline eGFRcr (positive, better-than-expected; negative, worse-than-expected predicted kidney function).

(5) Physiology-guided feature selection, anchored on haemoglobin, albumin and the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), yields the intersected gap (mKFGint) from compact metabolite panels (40 to 98 metabolites).

Associations with cardiometabolic markers were examined in MetaCardis, and model performance was validated in the Canadian Longitudinal Study on Aging (CLSA; N = 9,958) and the German chronic kidney disease (GCKD) study (N = 5,113) to predict myocardial infarction, stroke, all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, kidney failure, acute kidney injury, and 3-/4-point major adverse cardiovascular events in GCKD, as well as kidney disease incidence, incident myocardial infarction, incident type 2 diabetes, cerebrovascular disease incidence, and unplanned hospitalization in CLSA.
(B) Creatinine-based eGFR (eGFRcr) sits at the intersection of the cardiovascular, kidney and metabolic axes.

Physiologyguided optimisation tunes mKFGint toward three cross-axis CKM markers, haemoglobin (erythropoietic and kidney-cardiovascular link), albumin (nutrition and liver-kidney axis) and the neutrophil-tolymphocyte ratio (NLR; systemic inflammation), so that mKFGint serves as an integrated readout that is more sensitive than eGFRcr to CKM-syndrome biology and to downstream CKM events.
